title: How does a photo reach another phone?
hook: How does your photo cross the world in under a second?
caption: Your phone splits the photo into small data packets, sends them over Wi-Fi or mobile data to your provider, and they travel as pulses of light through fiber-optic cables, including undersea ones, to the app's server. The server forwards them to your friend's phone, which puts the pieces back together.

beats.say: You tap send, and a moment later your photo is on a phone across the world. How?
First, your phone chops the photo into thousands of tiny pieces called packets.
Each packet gets a label, like an envelope: where it's from, where it's going, and which piece it is.
The packets fly over Wi-Fi to your router, then into your internet provider's network.
From there, they travel as flashes of light through fiber-optic cables, some lying on the ocean floor.
The app's server receives the photo, and sends it on to your friend's phone through their network and a cell tower.
Their phone puts every piece back in the right order, and the photo appears.
Light in fiber covers about two hundred thousand kilometres every second. That's why it feels instant.

show.label: speed of light in optical fiber

title: Why is the sky blue?
hook: Sunlight is white. So why is the sky blue?
caption: Sunlight contains every colour. When it hits the tiny gas molecules in our atmosphere, short blue wavelengths are scattered in all directions far more than long red ones. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. At sunset, light crosses much more air, the blue is scattered away, and reds and oranges are left.

beats.say: Sunlight is white. So why is the sky blue?
White sunlight is actually every colour of the rainbow mixed together.
When it enters the atmosphere, it bumps into tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules.
Those molecules scatter short blue waves far more strongly than long red ones.
Roughly five to six times more. So blue light bounces around the whole sky and reaches you from every direction.
At sunset, light travels through much more air. The blue gets scattered away before it reaches you, leaving reds and oranges.

title: How does GPS know where you are?
hook: Your phone finds you to within a few metres, using clocks in space.
caption: GPS satellites orbit about 20,000 km up, each carrying atomic clocks and constantly broadcasting the exact time. Your phone measures how long each signal took to arrive, turns that into a distance, and with four or more satellites works out exactly where you are. The satellites' clocks even need corrections for Einstein's relativity.

beats.say: Your phone can find you to within a few metres, using clocks floating in space.
About thirty GPS satellites circle the Earth, twenty thousand kilometres up.

show.label: around 30 satellites in the GPS fleet

beats.say: Each one carries atomic clocks and keeps broadcasting: this is me, and this is exactly the time.
Your phone listens. The signal took a tiny moment to arrive, and that delay tells the distance to that satellite.
With distances to four or more satellites, there's only one point on Earth that fits. That's you.
And here's the wild part: the clocks must be corrected for Einstein's relativity, or GPS would drift by kilometres every day.

title: How does tap-to-pay work?
hook: Your card has no battery. So how does it pay when you tap?
caption: Contactless cards use NFC. The terminal creates a small radio field that powers the chip in your card, which has no battery. The chip then answers with your card details and a one-time code made just for this purchase, so copied data can't be reused. Phones do the same with a stand-in card number.

beats.say: Your bank card has no battery. So how does it pay when you tap it?
The terminal sends out a weak radio field, only a few centimetres wide.
Inside your card is a tiny coil. The field induces a current in it, and that powers the chip for a split second.
The chip answers with your card number, plus a one-time code made just for this purchase.
Because that code can't be used again, copying it is useless to a thief.
Phones and watches go one step further: they don't even send your real card number, just a stand-in.

title: How does a microwave heat food?
hook: A microwave doesn't heat the air. It shakes your food.
caption: A microwave oven makes radio waves at about 2.45 GHz. The electric field flips back and forth billions of times per second, and water molecules in the food keep twisting to line up with it. That jostling turns into heat. The waves reach a couple of centimetres in, and the rest of the food heats up by conduction, which is why stirring helps.

beats.say: A microwave doesn't heat the air. It shakes your food.
Inside is a magnetron, which makes radio waves at about two point four five gigahertz.
Water molecules are slightly charged at each end, so they twist to line up with the wave's electric field.
That field flips back and forth billions of times a second, so the water keeps twisting with it.
All that jostling turns into heat. But the waves only reach a couple of centimetres in.
The middle warms up by conduction, from the outside in. That's why the instructions tell you to stir.

title: How does a touchscreen feel your finger?
hook: Why does your screen ignore gloves, but notice your finger?
caption: Phone screens use capacitive touch. A grid of transparent conductive lines sits under the glass, holding a small electric charge. Your finger conducts electricity and changes the charge where you touch. The controller scans the grid many times per second to find exactly where that change happened. Ordinary gloves insulate your finger, so the screen can't feel them.

beats.say: Why does your phone screen ignore a glove, but notice your finger instantly?
Under the glass is a grid of see-through wires, holding a tiny electric charge.
Your body conducts electricity. When your finger gets close, it pulls a little charge away at that spot.
A controller scans every row and column many times per second, looking for that change.
Where a row and a column both change, that's exactly where you touched.
A glove insulates your finger, so the charge never changes. Touchscreen gloves have conductive thread in the fingertips.

title: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
hook: Your headphones fight noise by making more noise.
caption: Active noise cancellation uses microphones to listen to the sound around you. A chip creates a mirror-image sound wave, peaks where the noise has dips, and plays it through the speakers. The two waves cancel out. It works best on steady, low sounds like engines and fans, and less well on sudden or high-pitched noises.

beats.say: Noise-cancelling headphones fight noise by making more noise.
Tiny microphones on the outside listen to the sound around you, like a plane engine.
Sound is a wave of high and low pressure. The chip creates the exact mirror image of that wave.
The speaker plays that mirror wave. Where the noise pushes, it pulls, and the two cancel out.
It works best on steady, low sounds like engines and fans. Sudden or high sounds are harder to predict.

title: How does a 400-ton plane stay in the air?
hook: How does a 400-ton plane stay in the air?
caption: A wing is shaped and tilted so that it deflects air downward. Pushing air down pushes the wing up, and the air pressure above the wing ends up lower than below it. At take-off speed, that difference over a huge wing area is enough to lift hundreds of tons. Engines don't lift the plane, they keep it moving fast enough for the wings to work.

beats.say: How does a four-hundred-ton plane stay in the air?
It's all about the wings. They're shaped and tilted to push huge amounts of air downward.
Push air down, and the air pushes the wing up. Newton's third law.
At the same time, the pressure above the wing drops, while the pressure below stays higher.
A small pressure difference, spread over wings bigger than three tennis courts, adds up to hundreds of tons.
The engines don't lift the plane. They just keep it fast enough for the wings to do their job.

title: How does a QR code work?
hook: Why can a QR code still work when part of it is torn?
caption: QR codes were invented in 1994 by Denso Wave to track car parts. The three big squares tell the camera where the code is and which way it's turned. The small black and white squares are bits that spell out the data. Extra error-correction data is mixed in, so a code can still be read even when up to about 30% of it is damaged.

beats.say: A QR code can be scratched, torn, or have a logo in the middle, and your phone still reads it. How?
They were invented in Japan in 1994, to track car parts in factories.

show.label: by Denso Wave, for tracking car parts

beats.say: The three big squares in the corners tell your camera where the code is, and which way up it is.
Every small square is one bit: black is one, white is zero. Together they spell out a link or text.
The clever part is error correction: extra backup data mixed in, so missing pieces can be rebuilt.
At the highest level, a QR code still works with about thirty percent of it destroyed.

title: How does a fridge make cold?
hook: Your fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat.
caption: A fridge pumps heat out rather than making cold. A refrigerant flows in a loop: it evaporates inside the fridge and absorbs heat, a compressor squeezes the gas so it gets hot, the coils at the back release that heat into your kitchen, and an expansion valve drops the pressure so the liquid turns very cold again. That's why the back of a fridge feels warm.

beats.say: Your fridge doesn't make cold. It moves heat from inside to outside.
A special liquid called a refrigerant runs in a closed loop of pipes.
Inside the fridge, it evaporates into a gas, and evaporating soaks up heat from your food.
The compressor squeezes that gas, which makes it hot, hotter than your kitchen.
The coils at the back release that heat into the room. That's why the back of a fridge feels warm.
Then a valve drops the pressure, the refrigerant turns ice cold again, and the loop repeats.

title: How does Face ID recognise you?
hook: Your phone sprays your face with 30,000 invisible dots.
caption: Face ID projects more than 30,000 infrared dots onto your face. An infrared camera reads how the dot pattern is distorted to build a 3D depth map, which is turned into a mathematical model and compared with the one stored securely on your phone. Because it uses its own invisible light and depth, it works in the dark and isn't fooled by a flat photo.

beats.say: Every time you unlock your phone with your face, it sprays you with thirty thousand invisible dots.
The dots are infrared light. You can't see them, but a special camera can.
On a curved face, the dot pattern gets stretched and squeezed. That reveals a 3D shape.
The phone turns that shape into numbers, and compares it with the model it saved when you set it up.
Because it measures depth with its own light, it works in the dark, and a flat photo can't fool it.

title: How does a solar panel make electricity?
hook: How does sunlight turn into electricity with no moving parts?
caption: Solar panels are made of silicon cells with two layers that form a built-in electric field. When sunlight hits the silicon, its energy knocks electrons loose, and the field pushes them in one direction, creating a direct current. An inverter converts it to the alternating current your home uses. Typical panels turn about 20% of sunlight into electricity.

beats.say: A solar panel turns sunlight into electricity, with no moving parts at all. How?
Each panel is made of silicon cells, built from two layers that create an electric field between them.
Light arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons. When one hits the silicon, it knocks an electron loose.
The electric field pushes those freed electrons in one direction. Electrons moving together, that's a current.
An inverter changes it into the type of power your sockets use.
Most panels turn around a fifth of the sunlight that hits them into electricity.

title: Do websites know your password?
hook: A good website never knows your password. So how does it check it?
caption: Well-built sites don't store your password. They run it through a one-way hash function and store only the result, usually with a random salt added. When you log in, they hash what you typed and compare. If the database leaks, attackers get hashes, not passwords, but weak passwords can still be guessed, so use long, unique passwords and a password manager.

beats.say: A well-built website never knows your password. So how does it check you typed it right?
When you sign up, your password goes through a hash function: a one-way blender for data.
The same password always makes the same code. But you can't turn the code back into the password.
The site stores only that code, plus a random extra called a salt, so identical passwords look different.
When you log in, it hashes what you typed and compares the codes. Match, and you're in.
If hackers steal the database, they get codes, not passwords. But short passwords can still be guessed, so make yours long and unique.

title: What actually is lightning?
hook: Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
caption: Inside storm clouds, ice crystals and soft hail collide, separating electric charge: positive near the top, negative near the bottom. When the difference grows big enough, air breaks down and a giant spark jumps to the ground or another cloud. The channel heats to around 30,000 °C, and the air expands so fast it makes thunder. Light arrives first; sound travels roughly 1 km every 3 seconds.

beats.say: A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
It starts inside a storm cloud, where ice crystals and soft hail are thrown up and down and keep colliding.
Each collision swaps a little electric charge. Positive builds up at the top, negative at the bottom.
When the difference gets huge, the air itself breaks down, and a giant spark jumps.
The air heats so fast it explodes outward. That shock wave is thunder.
Light reaches you almost instantly, sound much slower. Count the seconds and divide by three: that's the distance in kilometres.

title: Why doesn't streaming video freeze?
hook: How does a movie play smoothly while it's still downloading?
caption: Streaming services cut each video into short chunks of a few seconds and encode every chunk at several quality levels. Your player keeps a buffer of upcoming chunks and measures your connection speed, picking higher or lower quality for each next chunk. The files sit on servers close to you, called a content delivery network, so they arrive quickly.

beats.say: How does a movie play smoothly while it's still downloading?
The video is cut into short chunks, just a few seconds each.
Every chunk is stored at several quality levels, from blurry to sharp.
Your player keeps downloading chunks ahead of where you are watching. That's the buffer.
It measures your speed constantly. Internet slows down? The next chunk comes in lower quality instead of freezing.
And the files come from servers in your own region, not the other side of the world.

title: How does a rainbow form?
hook: Why do you only see a rainbow with the Sun behind you?
caption: Each raindrop acts like a tiny prism. Sunlight enters the drop and bends, reflects off the back, and bends again on the way out. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the light fans out into a spectrum. The light comes back at about 42 degrees from the direction opposite the Sun, which is why rainbows are arcs and appear with the Sun behind you.

beats.say: Why do you only see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you?
Every raindrop acts like a tiny prism.
Sunlight bends as it enters the drop, reflects off the back, and bends again on the way out.
Each colour bends a slightly different amount, so white light fans out into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
The light comes back towards you at about forty-two degrees. All the drops at that angle form a circle around the point opposite the Sun.
The ground hides the bottom half, so you see an arc. From a plane, you can see a full circle.

title: How does your phone battery store energy?
hook: What actually moves inside your phone battery when you charge it?
caption: Lithium-ion batteries have two electrodes separated by a thin layer. Charging pushes lithium ions from the positive side into the graphite negative side, storing energy. When you use your phone, the ions flow back while electrons travel through your phone's circuits, powering it. Heat and long periods at 100% stress the materials, which is why batteries slowly lose capacity.

beats.say: What actually moves inside your phone battery when you charge it?
Inside are two layers, with a thin separator between them, soaked in a liquid that lets lithium ions pass.
Charging pushes lithium ions across, where they squeeze in between layers of graphite. That's stored energy.
When you use your phone, the ions drift back, and their electrons take the long way, through your phone's circuits.
Each trip wears the materials a little. Heat and sitting at one hundred percent make it worse.
That's why many phones now pause charging at around eighty percent overnight.

title: How does wireless charging work?
hook: How does power jump from the pad to your phone with no wire?
caption: Wireless chargers use electromagnetic induction. A coil in the pad carries alternating current, creating a changing magnetic field. A second coil in the phone sits in that field, and the changing field induces a current in it, which charges the battery. It only works over a few millimetres and loses more energy as heat than a cable, which is why alignment matters.

beats.say: How does power jump from a charging pad into your phone, with no wire?
Inside the pad is a flat coil of copper wire. Inside your phone, there's another one.
Current flowing back and forth in the pad's coil makes a magnetic field that keeps changing.
A changing magnetic field makes current flow in any coil nearby. That's induction, discovered nearly two hundred years ago.
But it only works over a few millimetres, and more energy turns into heat than with a cable.
That's why magnets in newer phones snap the coils into perfect alignment.

title: Why is it called Bluetooth?
hook: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king. Here's how it works.
caption: Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united rival tribes, just as the technology unites devices. Its logo combines his initials in runes. Bluetooth sends data by radio at 2.4 GHz and hops between many narrow channels many times per second, which avoids interference from Wi-Fi and other devices. Pairing exchanges secret keys so only your devices can talk.

beats.say: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king.
Harald Bluetooth united rival Danish tribes over a thousand years ago. The tech was meant to unite devices the same way.
It sends data by radio, in the same busy band as Wi-Fi and microwave ovens.

show.label: shared with Wi-Fi and microwave ovens

beats.say: To avoid all that noise, it keeps hopping between dozens of narrow channels, up to sixteen hundred times a second.
Both devices know the hopping pattern, so they jump together, and interference only hits a few hops.
Pairing exchanges secret keys, so only your devices can understand each other.

title: How does a search engine answer so fast?
hook: Search doesn't search the internet when you type. It already did.
caption: Search engines don't scan the web when you hit enter. Programs called crawlers constantly visit pages and follow links, and everything they find is organised into an index, like the index at the back of a book. Your query is looked up in that index across many servers at once, results are ranked by relevance and quality signals, and the answer comes back in a fraction of a second.

beats.say: When you hit search, it doesn't search the internet. It already did that.
Programs called crawlers visit billions of web pages, following link after link, all day long.
Everything they find goes into an index, like the index at the back of a book, but for the whole web.
Your search is split across thousands of machines, each checking its part of the index at the same time.
Results are ranked using hundreds of signals: relevance, freshness, links, and quality.
And all of that comes back to you in a fraction of a second.

title: How does your browser find a website?
hook: Computers don't understand website names. So how do they find them?
caption: Computers find each other by numeric IP addresses, not names. When you type a website name, your device asks a DNS resolver to translate it. If the answer isn't cached, the resolver asks a root server, which points to the server for the ending such as .com, which points to the server for that domain, which returns the IP address. This usually takes milliseconds and the answer is cached for next time.

beats.say: Computers don't understand website names. They only use numbers. So how does your browser find a site?
It asks the internet's phone book: the Domain Name System.
Your device asks a resolver, usually run by your provider: what's the number for this name?
If it doesn't know, it asks step by step: a root server, then the dot com servers, then the website's own server.
The answer comes back as a number, and your browser connects to it.
The whole lookup takes milliseconds, and it's remembered, so next time it's even faster.

show.label: a typical lookup, often less when cached

title: How does your phone know which way is up?
hook: There's a tiny moving weight inside your phone.
caption: Phones contain an accelerometer, a microscopic structure carved into silicon with a tiny mass held by springs. When the phone moves or tilts, the mass shifts slightly and the change in electrical capacitance is measured, revealing the direction of gravity and any acceleration. A gyroscope measures rotation. Together they rotate your screen, count your steps and steady your camera.

beats.say: There's a tiny moving weight inside your phone.
It's called an accelerometer: a microscopic structure carved into silicon, smaller than a grain of sand.
When you tilt or move the phone, that tiny mass shifts, just a little.
The phone measures that shift electrically, and works out which way gravity is pulling.
A second sensor, the gyroscope, measures how fast you're turning.
Together they rotate your screen, count your steps, and keep your videos steady.

title: The internet lives under the ocean
hook: Almost all of the internet between continents travels under the sea.
caption: Satellites carry only a small share of intercontinental internet traffic. The vast majority travels through more than a million kilometres of undersea fiber-optic cables. In the deep ocean they're about as thick as a garden hose, carrying light through glass fibers, with repeaters along the way that boost the signal. Ships lay them, and repair them when anchors or earthquakes break them.

beats.say: Almost all internet traffic between continents doesn't go through space. It goes under the sea.
Over a million kilometres of cables lie on the ocean floor, enough to wrap the Earth more than thirty times.
In the deep ocean, a cable is only about as thick as a garden hose.
Data travels through the glass as pulses of light, boosted by repeaters along the way.
Satellites carry only a small slice, because cables can move far more data, faster.
When anchors or earthquakes cut a cable, special ships haul it up from the sea floor and splice it back together.

title: How does a barcode work?
hook: A barcode doesn't store the price. So where does it come from?
caption: A typical product barcode simply encodes a number, using the widths of black bars and white spaces. The scanner shines light across it and measures the reflections, turning the pattern back into digits. The last digit is a check digit that catches mistakes. The store's computer then looks that number up in its database to find the product's name and price.

beats.say: A barcode doesn't store the price. So where does the price come from?
A product barcode is just a number, written in bars of different widths.
The scanner shines light across it. Black bars absorb it, white gaps reflect it.
The last digit is a check digit, calculated from all the others, so misreads are caught instantly.
Then the store's computer looks up that number, and finds the name and today's price.
That's why the same item can change price without ever changing its barcode.

title: How does your phone take photos in the dark?
hook: Night mode doesn't take one photo. It takes dozens.
caption: In the dark, a small phone sensor catches very little light, so a single short shot is noisy. Night mode captures a burst of many frames over a few seconds, aligns them to undo hand shake, and combines them. Random noise averages out while real detail adds up, giving a brighter, cleaner image, then software adjusts colour and tone.

beats.say: Night mode doesn't take one photo. It takes dozens.
In the dark, a tiny phone sensor catches very little light, so a single shot looks grainy.
So while you hold still, the phone captures a quick burst of frames over a few seconds.
Your hands shake a little, so software lines every frame up, pixel by pixel.
Random noise is different in every frame, so it averages away. Real detail is the same, so it adds up.
The result is one bright, clean photo, built from many dark ones.

title: How does your map app know about traffic?
hook: How does your map know there's a traffic jam ahead?
caption: Map apps learn about traffic mostly from phones on the road. Devices with location services send anonymised speed and position data. When many phones on the same road slow to a crawl, the app colours it red. Combined with historical patterns for that time of day, and incident reports, it estimates how long your trip will take and suggests faster routes.

beats.say: How does your map app know there's a traffic jam ahead?
Mostly, from other drivers' phones.
Phones with location turned on share anonymous speed and position data as they move.
When lots of phones on the same road slow to walking pace, that road turns red.
The app also knows how that road usually behaves at this hour, and adds reported crashes and road works.
Put together, it predicts your arrival time, and reroutes you around the jam.

title: Why are there two high tides a day?
hook: The Moon pulls the ocean, so why are there two high tides a day, not one?
caption: The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the side of Earth facing it and weakest on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: one towards the Moon, and one on the opposite side. As Earth rotates through both bulges, most coasts get two high tides and two low tides roughly every 24 hours and 50 minutes. When the Sun and Moon line up, tides are stronger.

beats.say: The Moon pulls the ocean towards it. So why are there two high tides a day, not one?
The Moon's gravity is strongest on the side of Earth facing it, and weakest on the far side.
That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges: one facing the Moon, and one on the opposite side.
Earth spins through both bulges every day, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides.
The Moon also moves along its orbit, so the cycle takes about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes.
When the Sun and Moon line up, their pulls add together, and you get extra-high spring tides.

title: How does Wi-Fi send data through the air?
hook: Wi-Fi is just radio. So how does it carry a whole movie?
caption: Wi-Fi is a form of radio, like FM, at much higher frequencies such as 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. Your router turns data into radio waves by changing their strength and timing in very precise patterns, each pattern standing for a group of bits. Your device's antenna catches the waves and decodes them. Modern Wi-Fi uses many channels and antennas at once to carry more data.

beats.say: Wi-Fi is just radio, like the radio in a car. So how does it carry a whole movie?
Your router talks at very high radio frequencies: two point four, five, or six gigahertz.
It turns bits into radio waves by changing their strength and timing, in very precise patterns.
Each pattern stands for a group of bits. Modern Wi-Fi packs ten bits into a single symbol.
Your phone's antenna catches the waves, and decodes the patterns back into data.
And it uses several antennas and channels at once, like adding lanes to a motorway.
